chapter.title: Inspecting the work: the 3 checks before you trust a build

cards.body:
Your builder says “All done!” Would you pay before walking through the house? Claude Code is that builder: skilled, fast, and just as cheerful about work nobody has checked.

**Before you trust a build, walk through it, read the list of jobs done, and leave a note for tomorrow's crew.**
cards.simpler: Your builder says “All done!” Would you pay before walking through the house? Claude Code is like that builder. It is skilled and fast. It also sounds just as cheerful about work nobody has checked. So before you trust what it built, do three things: **walk through it, read the list of jobs done, and leave a note for tomorrow's crew.**

cards.prompt: Claude finishes your birthday-countdown page and says: “Done! Everything works perfectly.” What's your next move?

options.text: Thank it and close the window. It said perfectly.
Open the page and use it yourself, the way a visitor would.
Ask it to say “perfectly” again, but more firmly.

whyNot.a: That's taking the builder's word, not checking the work: “done” means it stopped typing, not that you saw it run.
whyNot.c: That's asking for more confidence, not more proof: a louder “it works” is still not you seeing it work.

cards.reteach: A builder saying “finished” tells you they stopped working. Walking through tells you whether the taps run. Claude's “done” is its own report. Clicking through it yourself is the inspection.

cards.title: Checks one and two: try it, then make it explain
cards.body:
**Check one: use the app the way a stranger would.** Open it in your browser and click every button. Then do something a bit silly: leave a box empty, or type a word where a number should go. Builders test the doors they hung. Visitors lean on the railings.

Check two: ask Claude, “List every file you changed in this session and why, in plain words.” This is the *job sheet*, the builder's list of everything they touched. You don't need to read the code. Read the list and ask one question: did I ask for all of this?
cards.simpler: **First, use the app like a stranger would.** Open it in your browser and click every button. Leave a box empty, or type a word where a number should go. Builders test the doors they hung, but visitors lean on the railings. Second, ask Claude: “List every file you changed in this session and why, in plain words.” This is the job sheet. Skip the code. Read the list and ask: did I ask for all of this?

cards.title: The dinner that cost Infinity
cards.body: Sam builds a bill-splitter for a group dinner, and Claude says it's finished. Sam types $90 and 3 people and gets $30 each. Perfect. Then a friend types 0 people, and the page proudly announces that everyone owes “Infinity.” Sam asks for the job sheet, and Claude lists two changes: the splitter, plus a new page colour nobody asked for. That's two problems found in four minutes, before any real guest saw it.
cards.simpler: Sam builds an app to split a group dinner bill, and Claude says it's finished. Sam types $90 and 3 people and gets $30 each. Perfect. Then a friend types 0 people, and the page says everyone owes “Infinity.” Sam asks for the job sheet. Claude lists two changes: the splitter, and a new page colour nobody asked for. That's **two problems found in four minutes**, before any real guest saw it.

cards.prompt: Lena asked Claude to add a “clear all” button to her to-do app, and Claude says it's done. Which of these is a proper inspection?

options.text: Press “clear all” with 3 to-dos on the list, then with none, then ask Claude to list every file it changed and why.
Ask Claude “Did you test it?” and close the window when it says yes.
Open the main code file and scroll until it looks like plenty of code.

whyNot.b: That's the builder marking their own work, not your walk-through: you still haven't seen the button work.
whyNot.c: That's judging the house by the pile of wood, not by walking through it: more code doesn't mean the button works.

cards.reteach: An inspection is two things you do yourself. Use the new feature, odd cases included. Then read Claude's plain list of what it touched. Asking whether it works only gets you another “yes.”

cards.title: Check three: the note on the fridge
cards.body:
You'd think a builder this good would remember yesterday. Usually it doesn't. **Start a fresh Claude Code session tomorrow and it begins with none of today's chat.** Each new session, a fresh crew turns up at the site.

The fix is a plain text file called *CLAUDE.md* that lives in your project folder. Claude Code reads it on its own every time it starts there, like a crew reading the note taped to the fridge before they pick up a hammer. That way tomorrow's crew checks the work your way too.

Keep it short: 3 to 5 rules you really care about. “Explain every change in plain words.” “Ask me before adding a new service.” “Try an empty box before saying done.”
cards.simpler: You might expect such a good builder to remember yesterday. Usually it doesn't. **Start a fresh Claude Code session tomorrow and it remembers none of today's chat.** Each new session, a fresh crew shows up. The fix is a plain text file called CLAUDE.md in your project folder. Claude Code reads it every time it starts, like a crew reading a note on the fridge, so the next crew checks the work your way. Keep it short: 3 to 5 rules, like “Ask me before adding a new service.”

cards.body: On Monday, Jo tells Claude: “Always make buttons big enough for my thumb.” On Tuesday, in a fresh session, the buttons are tiny again. On Wednesday Jo types the rule again, a bit louder. Here's how to spot it: **if you've typed the same instruction in two different sessions, it belongs in CLAUDE.md, not the chat.**
cards.simpler: On Monday, Jo tells Claude: “Always make buttons big enough for my thumb.” On Tuesday, in a fresh session, the buttons are tiny again. On Wednesday, Jo types the rule again, a little louder. Here is the warning sign to watch for: **if you've typed the same instruction in two different sessions, put it in CLAUDE.md instead of the chat.**

cards.prompt: You've just finished a good session. Next week you start a brand-new Claude Code session in the same folder. Which of these can you count on it having?

options.text: The rules you typed into the chat an hour ago.
The rules written in the CLAUDE.md file in your project folder.

whyNot.a: That's the chat, not the notes file: a brand-new session starts without earlier conversations.
whyNot.c: That's the builder's report, not a note it reads: a new session doesn't start with it, and it was never a check anyway.

cards.reteach: Every new session is a new crew arriving at your house. They don't know what you told yesterday's crew. They only know what's taped to the fridge, and in Claude Code, that fridge note is CLAUDE.md.

cards.body: Open Claude Code in your project folder and type: “Create a CLAUDE.md with these 3 rules: explain changes in plain words, ask before adding new services, test with an empty box before saying done.” Then read the file.
cards.simpler: Open Claude Code in your project folder and type this: “Create a CLAUDE.md with these 3 rules: explain changes in plain words, ask before adding new services, test with an empty box before saying done.” When it's done, **read the file yourself** to see what it wrote.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Before you trust a build, use it like a stranger would, have Claude list what it changed and why, and write your rules into CLAUDE.md. The builder does the work; **you do the checking and keep the notes.**

Right now, only you can break this app. Soon you'll text a friend a link and watch them tap the one button you never tried.
cards.simpler: Before you trust a build, do three things. Use it the way a stranger would. Ask Claude to list what it changed and why. Write your rules into CLAUDE.md. The builder does the work, but **you do the checking and keep the notes.** Right now, only you can break this app. Soon you'll text a friend a link and watch them tap the one button you never tried.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now finish a session by testing the app yourself, reading Claude's list of what it changed, and writing 3 to 5 rules into CLAUDE.md for next time.

dubious_claims: 'Open Claude Code tomorrow and it starts with none of today's chat' is simplified. It's true for a fresh session, but `claude --continue` and `--resume` bring back the last chat, and Claude Code's auto-memory may save rules on its own. That makes the 'next week' recall exercise and Jo's Tuesday story a little less airtight.
Weaker one_idea point: check three (CLAUDE.md) is about memory across sessions, not checking the work. So exercise 3 tests a second idea rather than the same one from a new angle.
repairedFrom.why: The 'In one breath' card is all abstract summary with nothing to picture. Its teaser for the next chapter ('around day 14: putting an app online') reads like a schedule note, and it sits before the try card instead of at the end.
repairedFrom.fix: Make it the last card and close on a concrete hook: 'Right now only you can break this app. Next chapter, you text a friend a link and watch them find the Infinity bug you missed.'
